sections.name: Hook
lines: c_hook
You put your phone down on a pad, and it starts charging. No plug, no metal touching. So how does the power get across?
c_title
It's all magnets, in five steps.

sections.name: A coil in the pad
lines: c_coil
Step one. Inside the charging pad is a flat coil of copper wire, wound round and round like a spiral.
c_phonecoil
And inside your phone, just behind the back glass, is a matching coil.
c_ping
The pad stays quiet until it senses a phone. It sends out tiny test pulses, and only powers up when something answers.

sections.name: A flipping field
lines: c_field
Step two. The pad pushes electricity through its coil, and current in a coil makes a magnetic field.
c_flip
But the pad keeps flipping the current back and forth, more than a hundred thousand times every second.
c_pulse
So the magnetic field keeps growing, shrinking and flipping too, reaching up through the glass into your phone.

sections.name: Induction
lines: c_induce
Step three. Here's the trick. A changing magnetic field pushes electrons around any coil it passes through.
c_flow
So the field from the pad makes a current flow in your phone's coil, with no wires in between. That's called induction.
c_brush
It's the same idea in an electric toothbrush stand, and even in some kitchen hobs.

sections.name: Into the battery
lines: c_rect
Step four. That current flips back and forth too, but batteries need it flowing one way.
c_dc
So a chip in your phone straightens it out, and controls exactly how much goes into the battery.
c_talk
The phone and pad keep talking the whole time, asking for more power or less as the battery fills.

sections.name: Line it up
lines: c_align
Step five. The coils have to line up. Slide the phone off centre, and most of the field misses.
c_magnets
That's why some phones have a ring of magnets that snaps them into exactly the right spot.
c_heat
Even then, some energy is lost as heat, which is why wireless charging is a little slower and warmer than a cable.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
A coil in the pad. A field that flips. Induction makes a current in your phone. A chip feeds the battery. And the coils must line up.
outro
Next time your phone charges on a pad, you'll know it's catching a magnetic field. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
